title: Gender, Religion and Caste
subject: civics
syllabus_note: Follows the CBSE 2025-26 Social Science (087) syllabus: this chapter is fully in the board examination (Political Science: 20 marks). There is no map item from this chapter. NCERT figures (literacy 54% and 76%, Census 2001) are kept because the CBSE marking scheme uses them; newer Census 2011 and 2024 Lok Sabha figures are added for context.

blocks.title: Do differences divide us?
blocks.body:
Every society has differences: between women and men, between people of different religions, and between castes. In a democracy, these differences often show up in politics.

Is that good or bad? It can be both. When a group that was left out raises its voice, democracy becomes fairer. But when one group is turned against another, democracy is harmed. This chapter looks at three social differences: **gender, religion and caste**, and asks which expressions of them are healthy in a democracy.

blocks.title: Educate, and change society
blocks.body:
With her husband **Jotiba Phule**, **Savitribai Phule** opened one of the first schools for girls in India in Pune in **1848**. She became one of the country's first women teachers. People threw mud and stones at her on the way to school, but she carried a spare sari and kept teaching.

The Phules also fought against untouchability and caste discrimination. Their work shows how education can challenge both gender and caste inequality.
blocks.future: This chapter leads to careers in law, social work, journalism, public policy, teaching and gender and human rights studies.

blocks.question: When is it healthy for a social group to raise its demands in politics?
options: When a group that faces discrimination demands equal rights through democratic means
When one group demands that another group be kept out of power
Never: differences should not be expressed in politics
blocks.explanation: Expressing demands for equality is healthy; using differences to dominate or attack others is not.

blocks.title: Gender division, feminist movements and women's representation
blocks.body:
**Public/private division:** gender division is a form of hierarchical social division seen everywhere, but it is rarely recognised in the study of politics. It is understood as natural and unchangeable, but it is based not on biology but on **social expectations and stereotypes**.
- **Sexual division of labour:** a system in which all work inside the home is either done by the women of the family or organised by them through domestic helpers. Boys and girls are brought up to believe that the main responsibility of women is housework and bringing up children.
- Women do all the work inside the home, such as cooking, cleaning, washing clothes, tailoring and looking after children. Men do these jobs too when they are paid for it outside the home: most tailors or cooks in hotels are men.
- Many women also work outside: in villages they fetch water, collect fuel and work in the fields; in cities, poor women work as domestic helpers and middle-class women work in offices. But their work is **not valued** and does not get recognition.
- The result is that although women are about half of humanity, their role in **public life**, especially politics, is minimal in most societies.

**Feminist movements:** women in different parts of the world organised and agitated for equal rights. There were agitations in different countries for the extension of **voting rights** to women. These agitations demanded enhancing the political and legal status of women and improving their educational and career opportunities. More radical women's movements aimed at equality in **personal and family life** as well.
- A **feminist** is a woman or a man who believes in equal rights and opportunities for women and men.
- In some parts of the world, for example in **Scandinavian countries such as Sweden, Norway and Finland**, the participation of women in public life is very high.

**India: a patriarchal society.** **Patriarchy** literally means rule by father; it refers to a system that values men more and gives them power over women. Women in India face disadvantage, discrimination and oppression in many ways:
- **Literacy:** the literacy rate among women is only **54 per cent**, compared with **76 per cent** among men (NCERT figures, Census 2001; Census 2011 showed about 65 and 82 per cent). A smaller proportion of girls go for higher studies, because parents prefer to spend their resources on their sons' education.
- **Jobs:** the proportion of women among the highly paid and valued jobs is still very small. On average, an Indian woman works **one hour more** than an average man every day, yet much of her work is not paid and therefore often not valued.
- **Wages:** the **Equal Remuneration Act, 1976** provides that equal wages should be paid for equal work. However, in almost all areas of work, from sports and cinema to factories and fields, women are paid less than men, even when both do exactly the same work.
- **Son preference:** in many parts of India, parents prefer to have sons and find ways to have the girl child aborted before she is born. This sex-selective abortion led to a decline in the **child sex ratio** (number of girl children per thousand boys) to merely **919** (Census 2011). In some states, it fell below 850 or even 800.
- **Violence:** there are reports of harassment, exploitation and violence against women. Urban areas have become particularly unsafe for women, and even at home women face beating and other forms of **domestic violence**.

**Women's political representation:** issues of women's well-being do not get adequate attention because women's representation in legislatures is low.
- The percentage of elected women members in the **Lok Sabha** touched **14.36 per cent** for the first time in **2019** (78 women); in **2024**, 74 women were elected (about 13.6 per cent). Their share in many state assemblies is **less than 5 per cent**. India is among the bottom group of nations in the world in this respect.
- One way to solve this problem is to make it legally binding to have a fair proportion of women in elected bodies. This is what the **Panchayati Raj** has done: **one-third** of seats in local government bodies, in panchayats and municipalities, are reserved for women. There are now more than **10 lakh** elected women representatives in rural and urban local bodies.
- Women's organisations long demanded at least one-third of seats in the **Lok Sabha and State Assemblies** for women. In **September 2023**, Parliament passed the **Constitution (106th Amendment) Act (Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam)**, which reserves one-third of these seats for women; it will come into effect after the next census and delimitation.

Gender division is an example that some form of social division needs to be expressed in politics: disadvantaged groups benefit when social divisions become a political issue. In countries where women's political participation increased, their role in public life improved.

blocks.title: How women are disadvantaged in India
blocks.body:
| Area | What the facts show |
|---|---|
| **Education** | literacy rate of women 54% against 76% for men in the NCERT figures (Census 2001); Census 2011: about 65% against 82%. Fewer girls go for higher studies, as parents prefer to spend on sons |
| **Jobs and pay** | very few women in highly paid and valued jobs; an average woman works about one hour more than a man every day, but much of her work is unpaid and not valued; women are paid less despite the **Equal Remuneration Act, 1976** |
| **Son preference** | sex-selective abortion; child sex ratio fell to **919** girls per 1000 boys (Census 2011; it was 927 in 2001) |
| **Safety** | harassment, exploitation and domestic violence; public spaces are often unsafe for women |
| **Politics** | women were about **14 per cent** of Lok Sabha members in 2019 (78) and about 13.6 per cent in 2024 (74); less than 5 per cent in many state assemblies; one-third of seats in local bodies are reserved for women |

blocks.question: Who is a feminist?
options: A woman or a man who believes in equal rights and opportunities for women and men
Only a woman who works outside the home
A person who believes men are superior
A person who wants women to stay at home
blocks.explanation: Feminism is about equal rights and opportunities.

blocks.question: In India, one-third of seats are already reserved for women in:
options: the Union Cabinet
the Supreme Court
panchayats and municipalities
the Rajya Sabha
blocks.explanation: Reservation in the Lok Sabha and assemblies was passed in 2023 but comes into effect after the next census and delimitation.
option_feedback: There is no reservation in the Cabinet.

blocks.title: Communalism and the secular state
blocks.body:
Religious differences are often expressed in politics. Is that always wrong? Not necessarily:
- **Gandhiji** used to say that religion can never be separated from politics. By religion he meant not any particular religion, but the **moral values** that inform all religions. He believed politics must be guided by ethics drawn from religion.
- Human rights groups have argued that most of the victims of communal riots in our country are people from **religious minorities**, and have demanded that the government take special steps to protect them.
- Women's movements have argued that **family laws** of all religions discriminate against women, and have demanded that they be changed to make them more equitable.

These involve a relationship between religion and politics, and they are not wrong. Every person should be able to express in politics their needs, interests and demands as a member of a religious community. Those with political power should be able to **regulate the practice of religion** to prevent discrimination and oppression. These acts are fine as long as they treat every religion **equally**.

**Communalism:** the problem begins when religion is seen as the **basis of the nation**. It becomes acute when religion is expressed in politics in exclusive and partisan terms, when one religion and its followers are pitted against another, when beliefs of one religion are presented as superior, when demands of one religious group are formed in opposition to another, and when **state power** is used to establish the domination of one religious group over the rest. This manner of using religion in politics is **communal politics**.
- Communal politics is based on the idea that **religion is the principal basis of social community**. It believes that followers of a particular religion must belong to one community, that their fundamental interests are the same, and that people who follow different religions cannot belong to the same social community.
- This is a false belief: people of one religion do not have the same interests and aspirations in every context. Everyone has several other roles, positions and identities. There are many voices inside every community.

**Forms of communalism in politics:**
1. **Everyday beliefs:** routinely involve religious prejudices, stereotypes of religious communities and belief in the superiority of one's religion over others. This is so common that we often fail to notice it.
2. **Quest for political dominance:** a communal mind often leads to a quest for the political dominance of one's own religious community. For those belonging to the majority community, this takes the form of **majoritarian dominance**; for those belonging to a minority community, it can take the form of a desire to form a **separate political unit**.
3. **Political mobilisation on religious lines:** this involves the use of sacred symbols, religious leaders, emotional appeal and plain fear to bring the followers of one religion together in the political arena. In electoral politics, this often involves special appeal to the interests or emotions of voters of one religion in preference to others.
4. **Communal violence, riots and massacres:** sometimes communalism takes its most ugly form. **India and Pakistan** suffered some of the worst communal riots at the time of **Partition**, and the post-independence period has also seen large-scale communal violence.

**Secular state:** communalism was and continues to be one of the major challenges to democracy in our country. The makers of our Constitution chose the model of a **secular state**:
- There is **no official religion** for the Indian state. Unlike the status of **Buddhism in Sri Lanka**, that of **Islam in Pakistan** and that of **Christianity in England**, our Constitution does not give a special status to any religion.
- The Constitution provides to all individuals and communities **freedom to profess, practise and propagate any religion**, or not to follow any.
- The Constitution **prohibits discrimination** on grounds of religion.
- At the same time, the Constitution allows the state to **intervene in the matters of religion** in order to ensure **equality within religious communities**. For example, it bans **untouchability**.

Secularism is not just an ideology of some parties or persons; it is one of the **foundations of our country**. Communalism should be combated in everyday beliefs and in religion-based mobilisation in politics.

blocks.title: Forms of communal politics
blocks.body:
| Form of communal politics | Example |
|---|---|
| **Everyday beliefs**: religious prejudices, stereotypes and belief in the superiority of one's religion | thinking that people of another religion are all alike or inferior |
| **Quest for political dominance**: majoritarian dominance by the majority, or a separate political unit for a minority | demanding that the state follow one religion; demand for a separate state on religious lines |
| **Political mobilisation on religious lines**: sacred symbols, religious leaders, emotional appeal and fear | using religious slogans and fear of another community to win votes |
| **Communal violence, riots and massacres** | the riots at the time of Partition in 1947 |

blocks.question: Communal politics is based on the belief that:
options: all religions are equal
religion should guide politics through moral values
the state should protect religious minorities
religion is the principal basis of social community
blocks.explanation: Communal politics sees followers of one religion as one community with the same interests.
option_feedback: That was Gandhiji's view, which is not communal.
That is a demand of human rights groups, not communalism.

blocks.question: Which feature makes India a secular state?
options: Only the majority religion can be practised
There is no official religion for the Indian state
Hinduism is the state religion
The state never intervenes in religion
blocks.explanation: The Constitution gives no special status to any religion.
option_feedback: It can intervene to ensure equality, such as banning untouchability.

blocks.title: Caste inequalities, caste in politics and politics in caste
blocks.body:
**Caste inequalities:** unlike gender and religion, caste division is special to India. All societies have some social inequality and some form of division of labour, but in most societies occupations are not passed on from one generation to another. The caste system is an extreme form of this: it is based on **hereditary occupational division** sanctioned by rituals.
- Members of the same caste group were supposed to form a social community that practised the same or similar occupation, married within the caste group and did not eat with members of other caste groups.
- The caste system was based on exclusion of and discrimination against the 'outcaste' groups, who were subjected to the inhuman practice of **untouchability**.
- Political leaders and social reformers like **Jotiba Phule, Gandhiji, B.R. Ambedkar and Periyar Ramaswami Naicker** advocated and worked to establish a society in which caste inequalities are absent.

**Changes in modern India:** partly due to their efforts and partly due to other socio-economic changes, castes and the caste system have undergone great changes. With **economic development, large-scale urbanisation, growth of literacy and education, occupational mobility** and the weakening of the position of landlords in villages, the old notions of caste hierarchy are breaking down. In urban areas, it does not matter much who is walking along next to us on a street or eating at the next table in a restaurant. The **Constitution prohibited any caste-based discrimination** and laid the foundations of policies to reverse the injustices of the caste system.

**But caste has not disappeared:**
- Even now most people **marry within their own caste** or tribe.
- **Untouchability** has not ended completely, despite constitutional prohibition.
- The effects of centuries of advantages and disadvantages continue to be felt today. The caste groups that had access to education under the old system have done very well in acquiring modern education. Those groups that did not have access to education or were prohibited from acquiring it have naturally lagged behind. That is why there is a disproportionately large presence of **'upper caste'** among the urban middle classes. Caste continues to be closely linked to **economic status**.

**Caste in politics:** caste can take various forms in politics:
- When parties choose candidates in elections, they keep in mind the **caste composition of the electorate** and nominate candidates from different castes so as to muster the support needed to win.
- Political parties and candidates in elections make appeals to **caste sentiment** to muster support. Some political parties are known to favour some castes and are seen as their representatives.
- **Universal adult franchise** and the principle of **one-person-one-vote** compelled political leaders to gear up to the task of mobilising and securing political support. It also brought new consciousness among the people of castes that were hitherto treated as inferior and low.

**Caste alone does not decide elections:**
- **No parliamentary constituency** in the country has a clear majority of one single caste. So every candidate and party needs to win the confidence of more than one caste and community.
- **No party wins the votes of all the voters** of a caste or community. When people say a caste is a 'vote bank' of one party, it usually means that a large proportion of the voters from that caste vote for that party.
- Many political parties may put up candidates from the **same caste**, so some voters have more than one candidate from their caste while many voters have none.
- The ruling party and the sitting MP or MLA frequently **lose elections** in our country. That could not have happened if all castes and communities were frozen in their political preferences.
- Voters have strong attachment to political parties, which is often stronger than their attachment to their caste. People within the same caste or community have different interests depending on their **economic condition**. Rich and poor, or men and women from the same caste often vote very differently. People's assessment of the **performance of the government** and the **popularity rating of leaders** matter and are often decisive in elections.

**Politics in caste:** it is not politics that gets caste-ridden; it is caste that gets politicised:
- Each caste group tries to become bigger by incorporating within it neighbouring castes or sub-castes that were earlier excluded from it.
- Various caste groups are required to enter into a **coalition** with other castes or communities, and thus enter into a dialogue and negotiation.
- New kinds of caste groups have come up in the political arena, like **'backward' and 'forward'** caste groups.

**Effects:** caste politics has helped people from **Dalit and OBC** castes to gain better access to decision making. But **exclusive attention to caste can produce negative results**: it can divert attention from other pressing issues like **poverty, development and corruption**, and in some cases caste division leads to **tensions, conflict and even violence**.

blocks.question: Which of these shows that caste alone does not decide elections in India?
options: Some parties are known to favour some castes
Caste sentiment is used in campaigns
No parliamentary constituency has a clear majority of one single caste
Parties choose candidates keeping caste in mind
blocks.explanation: Every candidate must win support from more than one caste.
option_feedback: This shows caste matters in politics.
This shows caste matters in politics.
This shows caste matters in politics.

blocks.question: Exclusive attention to caste in politics can:
options: divert attention from issues like poverty, development and corruption
end untouchability at once
make every election peaceful
remove all economic inequality
blocks.explanation: This was the point of the 2025-26 sample paper assertion-reason question.
option_feedback: Untouchability needs social and legal action.
It can lead to tension and violence.

blocks.title: Memory tricks
blocks.body:
- **Women's disadvantages "LJWSV"**: Literacy, Jobs, Wages, Son preference, Violence.
- **Women's numbers "54-76, 919, 1976"**: literacy 54% vs 76% (NCERT), child sex ratio 919, Equal Remuneration Act 1976.
- **Four forms of communalism "Beliefs, Dominance, Mobilisation, Violence"** (B-D-M-V: "Bad Deeds Mean Violence").
- **Secular state "No-Free-No-Fix"**: No official religion, Freedom of religion, No discrimination, can Fix inequality within religions (untouchability ban).
- **Caste alone does not decide: "No majority, No full vote, Same-caste rivals, Sitting MPs lose".**
- **Politics in caste: "Bigger, Coalition, Backward-Forward".**

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.body:
1. Saying gender division is biological: it is based on **social expectations and stereotypes**.
2. Thinking only women can be feminists: a feminist is **a woman or a man** who believes in equal rights.
3. Calling every link between religion and politics communal: Gandhiji's moral values, protection of minorities and reform of family laws are **not** communal.
4. Saying a secular state has nothing to do with religion: it can **intervene** to ensure equality, such as banning untouchability.
5. Saying caste alone decides elections: no constituency has one caste majority, and sitting MPs often lose.
6. Writing that one-third reservation for women is already in force in the Lok Sabha: the 2023 Act will apply only after the next census and delimitation; it is in force in **panchayats and municipalities**.

blocks.title: Try this in class
blocks.body: Ask students to note who does each household task at home for one week (cooking, cleaning, shopping, paying bills, helping with homework). Pool the results anonymously and discuss: are these roles based on biology or on social expectations?

blocks.title: Think and explain
blocks.body: Think of an election advertisement or speech you have seen. Did it appeal to gender, religion or caste? Was the appeal for equality (healthy) or against another group (unhealthy)?

blocks.title: Where this leads
blocks.body:

- **Chapter 4 (Political Parties):** how parties mobilise voters.
- **Chapter 5 (Outcomes of Democracy):** dignity and freedom of citizens, especially women and disadvantaged castes.

blocks.title: Mastery challenge
blocks.body:
'Caste cannot alone determine election results in India.' Justify in about 120 words.

**Model answer:** Caste does play a role in politics: parties choose candidates keeping the caste composition of the electorate in mind and appeal to caste sentiment. But caste alone cannot decide results. No parliamentary constituency has a clear majority of one single caste, so every candidate must win the support of several castes and communities. No party gets the votes of all the voters of a caste. Many parties put up candidates from the same caste, so voters of that caste have to choose between them. Ruling parties and sitting MPs and MLAs frequently lose elections, which could not happen if caste preferences were fixed. Voters also judge the performance of the government and the popularity of leaders, and rich and poor members of the same caste often vote differently.

blocks.title: Chapter summary
blocks.body:
- Gender division is based on social expectations, not biology; the sexual division of labour keeps women's work unrecognised.
- Feminist movements demanded voting rights and equality; India is still patriarchal: low literacy, low pay, son preference and violence.
- Women's share in the Lok Sabha was about 14% in 2019; one-third of local body seats are reserved for women; a 2023 Act will reserve one-third in the Lok Sabha and assemblies.
- Communalism treats religion as the basis of the nation; its forms are everyday beliefs, quest for dominance, mobilisation on religious lines and violence.
- India is a secular state: no official religion, freedom of religion, no discrimination, and state intervention for equality.
- Caste still matters, but caste alone does not decide elections; politics has also changed caste, and exclusive attention to caste can be harmful.

blocks.title: Board exam tips
blocks.body:
- The 2025-26 sample paper had an assertion-reason item: exclusive attention to caste can produce negative results (answer: both true, R explains A), and a 2-mark question on two aspects of life where women face inequality (education, jobs, wages, son preference, violence).
- 3/5-mark favourites: forms of communalism, features of the secular state, caste inequalities today, why caste alone does not decide elections, women's representation.
- Use one fact or example in each point (54% literacy, Equal Remuneration Act 1976, child sex ratio 919).

blocks.back: Literally rule by father; a system that values men more and gives them power over women.
Politics based on the belief that religion is the principal basis of social community, using religion in exclusive and partisan terms.

blocks.front: Name four features of India's secular state.
blocks.back: No official religion; freedom to profess, practise and propagate any religion; no discrimination on grounds of religion; state can intervene to ensure equality within religions.

blocks.front: What is the sexual division of labour?
blocks.back: A system in which all work inside the home is done by women or organised by them through domestic helpers.
